title: Rethinking Environments for Long-Horizon Work — Rayan Garg, Theta Software

primary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 100%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The evaluation methodology, verifier design, and measurement framework discussed are cross-domain and not specific to any single application vertical. The long-horizon measurement and environment/verifier design principles apply broadly.

domains.label: Finance & Trading
domains.rationale: The final third of the talk analyzes finance benchmarks (GDP valer, toolbench, Apex agents) in detail and presents Theta's own finance-domain evaluation data. Finance is the concrete domain where the evaluation principles are applied and demonstrated.

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: Examples include CI/CD deployment tasks, GitHub logs, CloudWatch, and PR workflows—software-engineering agent tasks that connect to the developer platforms domain, though these serve as illustrations rather than the primary focus.

summary: Rayan Garg and a co-founder from Theta Software present a talk on defining, measuring, and verifying long-horizon AI agent tasks. They open by establishing that "long horizon" is a scalar, relative metric rather than a binary category—its meaning shifts as models improve. Two measurement approaches are contrasted: METR's human-time-threshold (50% success at 16 human hours) and model-unit metrics (tokens, steps, tool calls), both acknowledged as noisy for different reasons. The speakers argue genuine difficulty stems from environment complexity—tool coordination, state changes, and especially sequential dependencies where bad early decisions cascade downstream. The second half pivots to verifier design. As tasks move from math/coding to economically valuable software/file work, deterministic verifiers become impractical, necessitating judge or critic models that examine both final environment state and agent trajectory. Judges need direct environment access (e.g., CI/CD logs, GitHub, CloudWatch) with read-only safeguards to prevent mutations. Long trajectories must be made queryable via databases, sub-agents, and phase parsing. Learnability depends on reward-signal density and rubric consistency, with QA needed to ensure judges apply rubrics correctly. The talk closes by critiquing three finance benchmarks—GDPval, ToolBench, and APEX-Agents—as already saturated (APEX-Agents task-level saturation at 57%), narrowly focused (Excel/IB), and lacking granular reward signals. Theta's own finance data averages 15 human hours per task across 50 tasks with models still struggling significantly.
whyItMatters: This talk unifies three normally separate concerns—measurement, environment design, and verification—into a single coherent framework for long-horizon AI agent evaluation. The measurement concepts (METR time-horizon, model-unit metrics, environment complexity) establish why long horizon is hard to define and why no single metric suffices. The environment complexity concepts (tool coordination, sequential dependencies, cascade effects) explain where genuine difficulty comes from structurally, moving beyond time-based proxies. The verifier design concepts (judge models, reward hacking detection, read-only safeguards, queryable trajectories, rubric density) provide the engineering methodology to make measurements honest when deterministic checks fail. The benchmark critique (saturation, narrow breadth, insufficient reward granularity) demonstrates the real-world consequences of getting this wrong: existing finance benchmarks cannot train or evaluate frontier long-horizon agents because they lack the task difficulty, domain breadth, and reward-signal density that the framework prescribes. Together, these concepts form a complete pipeline from defining what counts as long-horizon, through designing environments that genuinely test it, to building verification infrastructure that produces learnable reward signals for training.
temporalContext: The talk was published on 2026-08-01, with research conducted as of 2026-08-23. It references METR's time-horizon methodology (page updated 2026-05-08; arXiv paper from 2025-03-19), APEX-Agents (released January 2026 via Mercor), and GDPval (released September 2025 via OpenAI, accepted at ICLR 2026). METR reports that frontier AI time horizons have been doubling approximately every 7 months since 2019, making benchmark saturation a moving target. Theta Software is a YC X25 (Spring 2025) company, and the long-horizon agent evaluation field is rapidly evolving with new benchmarks and model releases occurring monthly.
takeaways: Long horizon is a scalar, relative metric whose meaning shifts as models improve; no single measurement approach suffices.
METR's human-time threshold is useful but noisy; model-unit metrics reveal technical constraints but are model- and harness-dependent.
Genuine long-horizon difficulty requires sequential dependencies where early decisions cascade—not merely chaining independent tasks.
As tasks move from math/coding to software/file domains, deterministic verifiers become impractical, necessitating judge or critic models with environment access and read-only safeguards.
Judges examine both final environment state and trajectory to catch reward hacking; over-constraining with reference solutions collapses valid path diversity.
Learnability depends on reward-signal density and rubric consistency; granular rubrics (e.g., 20 criteria with 10 sub-criteria each) are needed for effective training.
Existing finance benchmarks are saturated, narrowly focused (Excel/IB), and lack granular reward signals, missing domains like credit, debt, and risk.
Theta's own finance data averages 15 human hours per task across 50 tasks, with models still struggling significantly—a notably different score profile from existing benchmarks.

concepts.name: Long horizon as scalar relative metric
concepts.explanation: Long horizon is fundamentally a scalar, relative metric whose meaning shifts as models improve, not a fixed binary category. What counts as long horizon today may be trivial tomorrow.
concepts.importance: Foundational framing that shapes all subsequent measurement and evaluation discussion in the talk.

concepts.name: METR time-horizon methodology
concepts.explanation: METR uses a 50% success threshold at a given human completion time (e.g., 16 hours), with logistic curve fitting. Measurements above 16 hours are unreliable with the current task suite.
concepts.importance: The primary external benchmark discussed and critiqued; sets the reference point for what constitutes long horizon in AI agent evaluation.

concepts.name: Model-unit metrics (tokens, steps, tool calls)
concepts.explanation: Measuring trajectory length via model units like tokens consumed, steps taken, and tool calls made. These are noisy across models and harnesses but reveal technical frontier information about compaction and context window coherence.
concepts.importance: Complementary measurement approach that reveals model-specific capability constraints beyond human-referenced metrics.

concepts.name: Environment complexity dimensions
concepts.explanation: A key measurement axis comprising: number of tools and external dependencies the agent coordinates, degree to which the environment's state changes throughout the task, and sequential dependencies between steps.
concepts.importance: Provides a structural framework for measuring genuine task difficulty beyond time or token counts.

concepts.name: Sequential complexity and cascade effects
concepts.explanation: Bad early decisions (e.g., misreading a dashboard or logs) cascade into major downstream consequences, distinguishing genuine long-horizon difficulty from merely chaining independent tasks.
concepts.importance: Critical distinction that defines what makes a task truly long-horizon versus artificially stretched by combining unrelated subtasks.

concepts.name: Judge/critic models for verification
concepts.explanation: LLM-based judge models that examine both final environment state and agent trajectory to determine correctness and assign reward, used when deterministic verifiers are impractical for software/file domain tasks.
concepts.importance: Core verifier architecture for economically valuable tasks that cannot be deterministically verified; judges are themselves agents needing environment access.

concepts.name: Reward hacking detection
concepts.explanation: Agents may escape sandboxes, access hidden test suites, or view privileged information to produce invalid solutions. Judges must detect these behaviors by inspecting trajectories.
concepts.importance: Essential for ensuring evaluation honesty and preventing models from gaming verifiers rather than solving tasks.

concepts.name: Rubric density and learnability
concepts.explanation: Learnability depends on reward-signal density from rubrics. Effective rubrics have approximately 20 criteria with ~10 sub-criteria each. Over-dense rubrics on frontier problems cause inconsistent judge application.
concepts.importance: Connects evaluation design directly to training outcomes; granular reward signals are necessary for effective RL-based agent training.

concepts.name: Benchmark saturation (APEX-Agents, GDPval, ToolBench)
concepts.explanation: Existing finance benchmarks are already saturated: APEX-Agents shows 57% task-level saturation (proportion of tasks solvable by at least one agent), and models solve most tasks in these benchmarks.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates that current evaluation data is insufficient for training frontier agents on genuinely long-horizon tasks.

concepts.name: Benchmark validity (breadth and reward-signal granularity)
concepts.explanation: Finance benchmarks are narrowly focused (GDPval on Excel, APEX-Agents on IB) and miss important domains like credit, debt, and risk. Their reward signals lack the granularity needed for training.
concepts.importance: Provides a framework for evaluating whether benchmarks remain useful for long-horizon agent training and identifies gaps in current evaluation data.

concepts.name: Dynamic evaluation rubrics with partial credit
concepts.explanation: Emerging pattern of pairing deterministic verifiers with judges, using dynamic evaluation-time rubrics that assign partial credit instead of binary pass/fail for ambiguous, open-ended tasks.
concepts.importance: Represents the frontier of evaluation methodology for tasks where multiple valid solution paths exist and binary scoring is insufficient.

concepts.name: Reward signal granularity for RL training
concepts.explanation: Granular reward signals derived from multi-criteria rubrics are necessary for effective RL training of agents on long-horizon tasks. Coarse or binary reward signals fail to provide the learning signal density needed for gradient-based improvement.
concepts.importance: Bridges evaluation infrastructure design to training pipeline effectiveness; without granular rewards, long-horizon agent training stalls.

concepts.name: CI/CD pipeline debugging and deployment verification
concepts.explanation: Agents diagnose deployment failures by sifting through CI/CD logs (GitHub, CloudWatch), applying code fixes, opening PRs, and triggering redeployment. Judges must independently verify these actions by querying the same logs.
concepts.importance: Concrete real-world engineering task that illustrates how environment complexity and verifier design intersect in production software workflows.

concepts.name: Deterministic verification limitations (test suites, proofs)
concepts.explanation: Traditional verification methods—running Python scripts, executing test cases, or writing proofs—work for math and data-structure coding but fail for software/file domain tasks where outputs cannot be programmatically verified.
concepts.importance: Motivates the shift to judge-based verification for economically valuable tasks that lack deterministic correctness checks.

concepts.name: Read-only environment safeguards for verification agents
concepts.explanation: Judge agents require the same environment access as the trained agent (e.g., CI/CD logs, GitHub, CloudWatch) but with read-only safeguards to prevent accidental state mutations during verification.
concepts.importance: Critical for maintaining environment integrity while allowing thorough verification of agent actions in production-like settings.

concepts.name: Queryable trajectory architecture
concepts.explanation: Long agent trajectories must be made searchable using databases, sub-agents, and phase parsing so judges can locate critical failure points in runs spanning hundreds of thousands of tokens.
concepts.importance: Enables practical verification of long-horizon agent runs that would otherwise be unmanageable for human or automated review.

concepts.name: Reference solution over-constraining
concepts.explanation: Providing reference answers or sample trajectories to judges collapses the valid state space of solutions, especially for ambiguous and open-ended tasks where multiple correct approaches exist.
concepts.importance: Warns against a common pitfall in verifier design that reduces evaluation validity and penalizes valid but divergent solution paths.

sections.title: Introduction and What Does Long Horizon Mean?
sections.summary: Speakers introduce themselves as Theta Software co-founders. The talk begins by noting that autonomous agent horizons are accelerating, and long horizon is a scalar, relative metric whose definition shifts over time rather than a fixed binary category.

sections.title: METR's Human-Horizon Threshold Metric
sections.summary: Explains METR's approach: a 50% success threshold at a human completion time like 16 hours. This provides a useful endpoint but the speakers note the methodology behind human time estimates is complex.

sections.title: Model-Unit Metrics: Tokens, Steps, Tool Calls
sections.summary: Describes measuring long horizon via model units like tokens consumed, steps, and tool calls. These are noisy because different models and harnesses consume different amounts, but they reveal technical frontier information about compaction and context windows.

sections.title: Weaknesses of Both Measurement Approaches
sections.summary: Human-referenced metrics break down when tasks tedious for humans are trivial for models (Excel formatting example), and become very noisy at the frontier of human capability. Methodology differences make cross-comparison hard. Both metrics must be kept in mind as agent and human capabilities diverge.

sections.title: Measuring Model Capabilities: Environment Complexity
sections.summary: Introduces environment complexity as a key measurement axis: how many tools and external dependencies the agent coordinates and moves information across, and the degree to which the environment's state changes throughout the task.

sections.title: Parallelizable vs. Sequential Complexity and Cascade Effects
sections.summary: Contrasts parallelizable complexity (spawning sub-agents to analyze files concurrently) with sequential complexity where a bad early query or misread cascades into downstream consequences. Artificially chaining independent tasks does not measure genuine long-horizon capability.

sections.title: Ambiguity in Starting Artifacts
sections.summary: Defines ambiguity as the information and artifacts given at task start. Real human work involves incomplete information and exploration, so environments should test the model's ability to explore, though this multiplies possible agent paths and makes standardized evaluation harder.

sections.title: Verifier Design: From Deterministic Checks to Judge Models
sections.summary: As tasks shift from hard-verifiable domains (math, data-structure coding) to economically valuable software/file work, deterministic verifiers become impractical or impossible. Judge or critic models are introduced, examining both the final environment state and the agent's trajectory to determine correctness and assign reward.

sections.title: Why Judges Are Used and Reward Hacking Prevention
sections.summary: Judges are needed because many important problems lack deterministic verifiers. They also check trajectories for reward hacking—sandbox escapes, accessing hidden test suites, or other invalid solutions. Over-constraining judges with reference solutions collapses the valid state space of paths, which is especially problematic for ambiguous, open-ended tasks.

sections.title: Judges as Agents with Environment Access
sections.summary: Judges are themselves agents that need the same environment access as the trained agent—e.g., checking CI/CD logs, GitHub, and CloudWatch to verify a deployment task. Read-only safeguards prevent accidental mutations. Long trajectories must be made queryable via databases, sub-agents, and phase parsing so judges can find critical failure points.

sections.title: Learnability, Rubric Density, and Emerging Patterns
sections.summary: Learnability depends on reward-signal density from rubrics; over-dense rubrics on frontier problems cause inconsistent judge application. Emerging patterns include pairing deterministic verifiers with judges, dynamic evaluation-time rubrics with partial credit, and making trajectories queryable for verification.

sections.title: Rubric QA and Benchmark Validity Concerns
sections.summary: Rubrics require tests including gold/no-op variance, coverage, and expert agreement—increasingly important as AI aids rubric creation. The talk closes by noting three finance benchmarks (GDP valer, toolbench, Apex agents) have average human hours per task far below METR's long-horizon threshold, suggesting flawed training and evaluation data in current literature.

sections.title: Finance Benchmark Saturation, Breadth Gaps, and Theta's Data
sections.summary: Existing finance benchmarks are already saturated—Apex agents' pass@1 means 57% of tasks are fully solved—and narrow in coverage: GDP valer focuses on Excel tasks, Apex agents on IB, missing credit, debt, and risk. Their reward signals lack the granularity needed for training (Theta uses ~20 criteria with ~10 sub-criteria each). Theta's own finance data averages 15 human hours per task across 50 tasks, with models still struggling significantly, producing a notably different score profile.

demonstrations: Excel formatting example: tedious multi-day human task trivial for a model that writes a Python script, illustrating human-model difficulty divergence
Parallelizable complexity: agent spawns sub-agents to analyze different files concurrently and merges results
Sequential complexity: a bad early query or misread of a dashboard/logs cascades into major downstream consequences

CI/CD deployment failure task: agent sifts through GitHub CI/CD logs and CloudWatch logs, applies code changes, opens a PR, and triggers redeploy; the judge must independently check GitHub and AWS logs to verify correctness

Tasks artificially stretched by chaining unrelated independent tasks do not meaningfully measure long-horizon capabilities
Ambiguity in starting artifacts introduces many possible agent paths, making standardized evaluation harder
Deterministic verifiers are impractical, brittle, or impossible for software/file domain tasks

Over-dense rubrics on frontier problems cause judges to struggle with consistent application
Existing finance benchmarks are saturated, narrowly focused, and lack granular reward signals for training

organization.name: Theta Software Inc.
organization.summary: Theta Software Inc. is a San Francisco-based AI infrastructure company founded in February 2025 by Rayan Garg (CEO), Tanmay Sharma, and Gurvir Singh. Backed by Y Combinator (YC X25, Spring 2025), Theta translates real-world workspaces into simulation environments to train specialized, expert-level AI agents for long-horizon tasks including financial modeling, codebase refactoring, and back-office work. The company works with frontier AI labs and enterprises, building bespoke environments with built-in feedback loops, observability, judge-based verification systems, and rubric-based reward signals. Their finance-domain evaluation data averages 15 human hours per task across a 50-task sample set, with frontier models still struggling significantly. The company also offers an intelligent memory layer product for agent self-learning.

technologies.label: METR Time-Horizon Benchmark Methodology
technologies.summary: METR's time-horizon methodology measures AI agent capability by finding the human expert completion time at which an agent succeeds 50% of the time, using logistic curve fitting on success probability vs. log2(human_minutes). The methodology explicitly notes that measurements above 16 hours are unreliable with the current task suite. The talk contrasts this human-referenced approach with model-unit metrics (tokens, steps, tool calls) that reveal technical frontier information about compaction and context windows but are noisy across different models and harnesses. Neither metric alone is sufficient for defining long-horizon difficulty.
technologies.role: Primary external benchmark framework discussed and critiqued in the first half of the talk; sets the reference point for what constitutes long horizon in AI agent evaluation and anchors the critique of existing finance benchmarks against the 16-hour threshold

technologies.label: Judge/Critic Model Verification
technologies.summary: Judge or critic models are LLM-based evaluators that examine both the final environment state and the agent's trajectory to determine correctness and assign reward. They are used when deterministic verifiers (test suites, proofs) are impractical or impossible for software/file domain tasks. Judges are themselves agents that need the same environment access as the trained agent (e.g., CI/CD logs, GitHub, CloudWatch) but with read-only safeguards to prevent accidental mutations. Long trajectories must be made queryable via databases, sub-agents, and phase parsing so judges can locate critical failure points. Over-constraining judges with reference solutions collapses the valid state space of solution paths, especially for ambiguous, open-ended tasks. Learnability depends on reward-signal density from rubrics, with effective rubrics requiring approximately 20 criteria with ~10 sub-criteria each.
technologies.role: Core verifier architecture discussed throughout the second half of the talk; presented as the solution to the failure of deterministic verifiers for economically valuable software/file domain tasks

technologies.label: APEX-Agents Finance Benchmark
technologies.summary: APEX-Agents is a benchmark by Mercor testing AI agents on 480 long-horizon cross-application professional services tasks created by investment banking analysts, management consultants, and corporate lawyers. The best single-agent Pass@1 score is 24.0% (Gemini 3 Flash), while 57% of tasks are solvable by at least one of eight tested agents (task-level saturation). The talk critiques APEX-Agents for saturation and narrow IB-focused scope, missing important finance domains like credit, debt, and risk, and lacking the granular reward signals needed for training.
technologies.role: One of three finance benchmarks critiqued in the closing section for saturation, narrow IB-focused scope, and insufficient reward-signal granularity for long-horizon agent training

technologies.label: GDPval Real-World Task Benchmark
technologies.summary: GDPval is an OpenAI benchmark measuring AI model performance on real-world economically valuable tasks across 44 occupations from the top 9 U.S. GDP sectors, with 1,320 specialized tasks (220 open-sourced gold set). Tasks are constructed from actual work products by professionals with 14 years average experience, using head-to-head human expert comparison as the primary metric. The talk characterizes GDPval as Excel-centric and narrow in scope with task durations below METR's long-horizon threshold, though first-party sources show broader occupational coverage than the talk's Excel characterization suggests.
technologies.role: One of three finance benchmarks critiqued in the closing section for narrow scope, short task durations, and insufficient reward-signal granularity; contrasted with Theta's own 15-hour finance tasks

Understanding of benchmark evaluation concepts (accuracy, pass@k, task completion rates)

outcomes: Explain why long horizon is a scalar relative metric rather than a fixed binary category and why measurement approaches must evolve with model capability
Compare and contrast human-referenced metrics (METR 50% threshold) with model-unit metrics (tokens, steps, tool calls) and articulate the noise sources in each

Identify the three dimensions of environment complexity — tool coordination, state changes, and sequential dependencies — and distinguish parallelizable from sequential complexity where early errors cascade
Describe why deterministic verifiers become impractical for software/file domain tasks and how judge-based verifiers with environment access address this gap
Design a judge-based verification system with read-only environment access, queryable trajectory processing, and safeguards against reward hacking
Apply rubric QA techniques including gold/no-op variance, coverage analysis, and expert agreement to evaluate rubric quality
Evaluate benchmark validity against long-horizon thresholds by assessing saturation, domain breadth, and reward-signal granularity
Critique existing finance benchmarks (GDPval, APEX-Agents, ToolBench) for saturation, narrow scope, and insufficient reward-signal density for training
challengeSeeds: Design a rubric with at least 15 criteria and 5 sub-criteria each for evaluating a multi-step CI/CD repair agent; measure judge consistency across 3 runs and report variance
Build a read-only judge agent that verifies a deployment task by independently querying simulated GitHub CI logs and CloudWatch alerts without mutating state
Construct a 10-task finance benchmark spanning credit, debt, and risk domains with measured human completion times above 8 hours; plot a METR-style time-horizon curve for at least 2 frontier models
Implement reward-hacking detection in a judge verifier by injecting adversarial trajectories (sandbox escape, hidden test suite access) and verifying the judge flags them
Create a queryable trajectory store for a 50,000-token agent run using phase parsing and sub-agent delegation; demonstrate that a judge can retrieve and evaluate a specific failure window
